claims.claim: The Institute of Medicine (1990) defined quality of care as the degree to which health services for individuals and populations increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge.
The IOM report Crossing the Quality Chasm (2001) named six aims for improvement: care should be safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable.

In Crossing the Quality Chasm, 'effective' means providing services based on scientific knowledge to all who could benefit and refraining from providing them to those not likely to benefit (avoiding underuse and overuse); 'equitable' means care that does not vary in quality because of personal characteristics such as gender, ethnicity, geographic location, and socioeconomic status.

Avedis Donabedian's framework (1966, elaborated 1988) organizes quality assessment into three linked categories: structure (the settings and resources of care), process (what is done for patients), and outcome (the effect on patient health).
Quality measures are commonly classified as structure, process, outcome, or patient-reported outcome measures, mirroring the Donabedian categories.

The National Quality Forum (NQF) is a private, nonprofit, consensus-based organization that endorses standardized performance measures through a multi-stakeholder consensus development process; endorsed measures were long treated as a gold standard and given privileged status in federal reporting programs.

NQF's federal role has changed: in 2023 it became an affiliate of The Joint Commission, and CMS ended NQF's roughly 15-year contract as the federal consensus-based entity for endorsing performance measures.

AHRQ maintains the AHRQ Quality Indicators, standardized measures computed from hospital administrative discharge data, grouped into modules including Prevention Quality Indicators (PQIs), Inpatient Quality Indicators (IQIs), Patient Safety Indicators (PSIs), and Pediatric Quality Indicators (PDIs).
CMS runs value-based programs that tie a portion of payment to quality-measure performance rather than volume of services, in contrast to traditional fee-for-service payment.

Quality assurance is conceptually a retrospective, inspection-based approach that checks whether performance meets a fixed threshold or standard, while quality improvement (CQI/TQM) is a prospective, continuous approach that raises performance toward goals rather than settling at a threshold.
Value in health care is expressed as quality (or health outcomes) relative to the cost of achieving it, which is why measuring quality is a prerequisite for value-based purchasing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Timing and nature of the NQF–Joint Commission arrangement and NQF's federal role
positions: Trade press described a 2023–2024 'affiliation' with The Joint Commission, with NQF remaining an independent entity within the enterprise
Some coverage framed the same change as an acquisition/merger; separately, CMS ended NQF's long-standing consensus-based-entity contract
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the durable, verifiable facts — NQF is a private nonprofit consensus-based measure endorser whose federal CBE role has since transitioned — and avoids asserting a precise merger date or the identity of the successor entity, which are not needed for a conceptual lesson.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced all placeholder boilerplate with sourced substance on the IOM definition, the six aims, the Donabedian framework, measure types, measure stewards, QA vs QI, and value.
Attributed the six aims to IOM (2001) and the structure–process–outcome framework to Avedis Donabedian, per assignment.
Kept improvement methodology, patient-safety mechanics, and root cause analysis out of scope to avoid duplication with sibling topics.
rightsIssues: Donabedian (1988) is a copyrighted JAMA article — REFERENCE_ONLY; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.
NQF, Joint Commission, and AHRQ materials are cited and described; no standards text reproduced.
IOM/NASEM reports are copyrighted; the six-aim definitions are short factual definitions re-expressed and attributed, not block-quoted.

sourceRecords.title: Crossing the Quality Chasm: A New Health System for the 21st Century (Executive Summary)
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative source for the six aims for improvement (safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, equitable) and their one-line IOM definitions, read via the NCBI Bookshelf reprint of the 2001 IOM report. Also supports the 'chasm' framing (gap between care we have and care we could have). Definitions re-expressed in original prose; not block-quoted.

sourceRecords.title: Measuring the Quality of Health Care (citing IOM 1990, Medicare: A Strategy for Quality Assurance)
sourceRecords.notes: Source of the widely used IOM (1990) definition of quality: 'the degree to which health services for individuals and populations increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge.' Definition confirmed via web search of NAP/NCBI copies; original definition is from IOM, Medicare: A Strategy for Quality Assurance (1990).

sourceRecords.title: The Quality of Care: How Can It Be Assessed?
sourceRecords.notes: Foundational article (JAMA 1988;260(12):1743–1748) establishing the structure–process–outcome framework, building on Donabedian's 1966 Milbank article. Attributed to Avedis Donabedian per assignment. Copyrighted — facts and framework synthesized in original wording; abstract/citation confirmed via PubMed.

sourceRecords.title: National Quality Forum (StatPearls)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports NQF as a private nonprofit with 400+ member bodies using a consensus development process to endorse performance measures submitted by developers such as CMS and NCQA; endorsed measures treated as a gold standard and given privileged status in federal programs; roughly half of federal quality measures were NQF-endorsed. Also supports measure-type categories (outcome, process, patient-reported outcome, cost, structure). Read via NCBI Bookshelf.

sourceRecords.title: The Joint Commission and NQF Form Affiliation
sourceRecords.notes: Secondary trade coverage used only to support the durable fact that NQF affiliated with The Joint Commission (2023) and that CMS ended NQF's long-standing federal consensus-based-entity contract. Precise merger date and successor entity intentionally not asserted in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: AHRQ Quality Indicators
sourceRecords.provider: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports AHRQ QIs as standardized measures derived from hospital administrative/discharge data, grouped into modules — Prevention Quality Indicators (PQIs), Inpatient Quality Indicators (IQIs), Patient Safety Indicators (PSIs), Pediatric Quality Indicators (PDIs), plus newer maternal-health measures. Module purposes confirmed via AHRQ web pages and the AHRQ QI brochure. US government work.

sourceRecords.title: Quality Assurance (StatPearls)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the conceptual QA-vs-QI contrast: QA as retrospective, inspection-based, threshold-meeting; CQI/TQM as prospective, continuous, goal-raising. Notes the 1990s shift and the Joint Commission's 1992 move to promote CQI. Read via NCBI Bookshelf; used only for the conceptual distinction, not for improvement methodology (which is out of scope).

sourceRecords.title: CMS' Value-Based Programs
sourceRecords.notes: Official CMS page framing value-based payment as rewarding quality of care rather than volume of services, in contrast to traditional fee-for-service. Reused from the shared source registry; read via curl with a browser user-agent.
